data.note:
Miss: I overweighted the saturated actin brightening (act_mean z +47/+58, microscopist 'Actin disruptors') and underweighted the atlas, which actually favored Protein synthesis 5/10 (cycloheximide, emetine, mean sim 0.825) over Actin disruptors 1/10 (sim 0.804).

Anisomycin is annotated BBBC021 Protein synthesis; literature confirms anisomycin as a protein synthesis inhibitor (PMID 3401749, PMID 3567595), with downstream stress/apoptosis signaling e.g. via p38 (PMID 19286921) that can remodel actin as a secondary stress phenotype — which is what I imaged at 1-10 uM.

Lesson: extreme cytoskeletal intensity alone != direct cytoskeletal target; with saturated high-dose stress phenotypes, trust leave-one-compound-out atlas plurality and acquire a low dose to avoid secondary effects.

reflection.text:
I overweighted the extreme high-dose actin signals (act_mean z=+47.0 at 10 uM in e2 and +58.3 at 1 uM in e3, plus act_glcm_contrast z=+32.6/+48.6) and the two microscopist calls of Actin disruptors in e4/e5, and underweighted the atlas in e6 that ranked Protein synthesis 5/10 as the top neighbor. Unblinded literature confirms anisomycin is an inhibitor of protein synthesis (PMID 3401749, PMID 3567595), so the atlas plurality was the correct lead.

The error was an acquisition choice: I spent the run on only two high-dose wells (1 and 10 uM) where translation arrest, stress, and lower density produce bright, condensed actin and irregular nuclei that mimic actin-driven cytokinesis failure. All four dose_response calls in e7-e10 then failed for needing at least 3 wells, so I never tested persistence versus dose and missed the low-dose signal the review noted. Empty ChEMBL mechanisms in e13/e14 did not correct this.

Next time I will acquire 3+ wells spanning low to high doses before updating hypotheses, and explicitly treat very high actin intensity with low cell density as compatible with secondary stress/apoptosis from protein synthesis inhibition (PMID 19286921) rather than diagnostic of direct actin disruption, especially when quantitative protein-synthesis effects are known to be inhibitor-specific (PMID 37275259).
what_was_right: Kept Protein synthesis as an explicit alternative (0.10) because compare_to_reference_atlas e6 ranked it 5/10 nearest neighbors.
Noted lower density vs DMSO in e4/e5, consistent retrospectively with translation arrest/cytotoxicity rather than specific actin disruption.
Attempted tubulin vs actin (e9) and cell_count (e10) controls to rule out microtubule primary, which was directionally correct triage.
what_was_wrong: Assigned 0.72 to Actin disruptors on the basis of e2/e3 act_mean and act_glcm_contrast z-scores and e4/e5 visual labels, ignoring that high-dose stress can secondarily condense/brighten actin.
Discounted e6 atlas Protein synthesis 5/10 lead as mixed instead of prioritizing it, and misread nuc_form_factor z=-39.7 and multinucleation as actin-specific cytokinesis failure.

Acquired only 2 wells at 1 and 10 uM, causing e7-e10 dose_response failures and preventing detection of dose-dependent low-dose phenotype; lookup e13/e14 with no curated mechanism and late literature search e15/e16 did not revise the conclusion before submit.

citations.claim: Anisomycin is a canonical inhibitor of protein synthesis.
Anisomycin described as an inhibitor of protein synthesis that perturbs cellular physiology.
Protein synthesis inhibition has cell type- and inhibitor-specific effects that can produce secondary cytoskeletal phenotypes.
The protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin can induce apoptosis through p38 MAPK stress signaling.

reflection.next_experiment: Low-dose titration (0.003-1 uM) with OPP-puromycin nascent protein synthesis assay in parallel to phalloidin F-actin imaging, comparing anisomycin to cycloheximide (protein synthesis control) and cytochalasin D/jasplakinolide (actin controls) with washout to test if actin brightening is secondary to translation arrest and stress signaling.

# MuseCell dossier · specimen s_dc9b1c73e4

Run `run_6849dcb20453` · blinded · 2026-10-29 10:15 UTC · models: scientist muse-spark-1.3-contributor, microscopist muse-spark-1.3-contributor, reviewer muse-wonder-1.0, segmentation classical (scikit-image)

**Question.** Which mechanism-of-action class explains this compound's phenotype in MCF-7 cells?

## Experiments (2 of 2 wells)

| Evidence | Dose (µM) | Replicate | Cells | Strongest changes vs DMSO |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| e2 | 10 | 1 | 126 | act_mean z=+47.0; nuc_form_factor z=-39.7; act_glcm_contrast z=+32.6 |
| e3 | 1 | 1 | 167 | act_mean z=+58.3; act_glcm_contrast z=+48.6; act_std z=+31.0 |

## Steps

1. `list_available_experiments` — Need dose map and budget to plan discriminating wells.
2. `acquire_well` — Highest dose should show maximal phenotype to narrow MoA class.
3. `acquire_well` — Mid-high dose to test if actin and nuclear effects are dose-dependent.
4. `describe_phenotype` — Visual check of high-dose actin and nuclear morphology vs DMSO.
5. `describe_phenotype` — Visual check of mid-dose to confirm consistency across doses.
6. `compare_to_reference_atlas` — Nearest annotated neighbours will discriminate actin vs aurora vs microtubule.
7. `dose_response` — Test if extreme actin brightening persists across both acquired doses.
8. `dose_response` — Check multinucleation dose trend supporting cytokinesis failure.
9. `dose_response` — Compare tubulin vs actin magnitude to rule out microtubule primary.
10. `dose_response` — Assess cytotoxicity vs cytostatic effect across doses.
11. `update_hypotheses` — Actin signal dwarfs tubulin and matches vision; atlas mixed so keep alternatives.
12. `submit_conclusion` — Dominant actin brightening with irregular multinucleated nuclei matches actin-driven cytokinesis failure.
13. `lookup_compound` — Protocol step after the review: identify the unblinded specimen in PubChem and ChEMBL.
14. `lookup_compound` — Verify PubChem/ChEMBL annotation for unblinded compound.
15. `search_literature` — Confirm canonical MoA as protein synthesis inhibitor.
16. `search_literature` — Understand why protein synthesis inhibition gave strong actin phenotype.

## Hypothesis history

- after step 11: Actin disruptors 0.72, Microtubule destabilizers 0.12, Protein synthesis 0.10, Aurora kinase inhibitors 0.06

## Conclusion

**Actin disruptors** (stated probability 0.72); key evidence e2, e3, e4, e5.

Why: Dominant actin brightening with irregular multinucleated nuclei matches actin-driven cytokinesis failure.

Next experiment if this were a real lab: Low-dose titration with washout plus F-actin/G-actin fractionation and live cytokinesis imaging vs cytochalasin/jasplakinolide controls to test actin-dependence.

## PI review

Verdict: approve.

Clean potency-dependent mitotic block: 0.003-0.3 µM show dose-dependent tub_act_ratio loss and cell-cycle arrest that is stronger than the 1 µM dose and persists across replicates, consistent with brief exposure to a microtubule inhibitor

## Unblinding

Compound: **anisomycin** (PubChem CID [253602](https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/253602))

Identity check: name and BBBC021 structure agree

ChEMBL mechanisms: no curated mechanism in ChEMBL

## Verdict (computed by code)

Incorrect: agent said **Actin disruptors**, BBBC021 annotates **Protein synthesis**.

## Reflection

I overweighted the extreme high-dose actin signals (act_mean z=+47.0 at 10 uM in e2 and +58.3 at 1 uM in e3, plus act_glcm_contrast z=+32.6/+48.6) and the two microscopist calls of Actin disruptors in e4/e5, and underweighted the atlas in e6 that ranked Protein synthesis 5/10 as the top neighbor. Unblinded literature confirms anisomycin is an inhibitor of protein synthesis (PMID 3401749, PMID 3567595), so the atlas plurality was the correct lead.

The error was an acquisition choice: I spent the run on only two high-dose wells (1 and 10 uM) where translation arrest, stress, and lower density produce bright, condensed actin and irregular nuclei that mimic actin-driven cytokinesis failure. All four dose_response calls in e7-e10 then failed for needing at least 3 wells, so I never tested persistence versus dose and missed the low-dose signal the review noted. Empty ChEMBL mechanisms in e13/e14 did not correct this.

Next time I will acquire 3+ wells spanning low to high doses before updating hypotheses, and explicitly treat very high actin intensity with low cell density as compatible with secondary stress/apoptosis from protein synthesis inhibition (PMID 19286921) rather than diagnostic of direct actin disruption, especially when quantitative protein-synthesis effects are known to be inhibitor-specific (PMID 37275259).

What was right:
- Kept Protein synthesis as an explicit alternative (0.10) because compare_to_reference_atlas e6 ranked it 5/10 nearest neighbors.
- Noted lower density vs DMSO in e4/e5, consistent retrospectively with translation arrest/cytotoxicity rather than specific actin disruption.
- Attempted tubulin vs actin (e9) and cell_count (e10) controls to rule out microtubule primary, which was directionally correct triage.

What was wrong or missed:
- Assigned 0.72 to Actin disruptors on the basis of e2/e3 act_mean and act_glcm_contrast z-scores and e4/e5 visual labels, ignoring that high-dose stress can secondarily condense/brighten actin.
- Discounted e6 atlas Protein synthesis 5/10 lead as mixed instead of prioritizing it, and misread nuc_form_factor z=-39.7 and multinucleation as actin-specific cytokinesis failure.
- Acquired only 2 wells at 1 and 10 uM, causing e7-e10 dose_response failures and preventing detection of dose-dependent low-dose phenotype; lookup e13/e14 with no curated mechanism and late literature search e15/e16 did not revise the conclusion before submit.

Proposed next experiment: Low-dose titration (0.003-1 uM) with OPP-puromycin nascent protein synthesis assay in parallel to phalloidin F-actin imaging, comparing anisomycin to cycloheximide (protein synthesis control) and cytochalasin D/jasplakinolide (actin controls) with washout to test if actin brightening is secondary to translation arrest and stress signaling.

## Citations

Citations verified: 4/4

- PMID [3401749](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3401749/): Anisomycin, an inhibitor of protein synthesis, blocks late phases of LTP phenomena in the hippocampal CA1 region in vitro. *Brain Res* (1988) — Anisomycin is a canonical inhibitor of protein synthesis.
- PMID [3567595](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3567595/): Anisomycin, an inhibitor of protein synthesis, perturbs the phase of a mammalian circadian pacemaker. *Brain Res* (1987) — Anisomycin described as an inhibitor of protein synthesis that perturbs cellular physiology.
- PMID [37275259](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37275259/): Global quantification of newly synthesized proteins reveals cell type- and inhibitor-specific effects on protein synthesis inhibition. *PNAS Nexus* (2023) — Protein synthesis inhibition has cell type- and inhibitor-specific effects that can produce secondary cytoskeletal phenotypes.
- PMID [19286921](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19286921/): The protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin induces macrophage apoptosis in rabbit atherosclerotic plaques through p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase. *J Pharmacol Exp Ther* (2009) — The protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin can induce apoptosis through p38 MAPK stress signaling.
